landing.hero.headline: AI Room Design: Redesign Any Room From One Photo
landing.hero.subheadline: Upload a photo of your room and get a photorealistic AI design in about 20 seconds. Pick from eight curated styles — Modern, Scandinavian, Japandi, Industrial and more — and the AI redesigns your space while keeping your real walls, windows and lighting intact. Your first design is free after sign-up; credits from $5 for clean downloads.
landing.hero.results_hint: Every image here started as a single photo — drag the slider in the gallery below
landing.gallery.title: Real rooms. Real results.
landing.gallery.subtitle: Every image below was generated from a single photo. Drag the slider to see the before and after.
landing.how.title: How to Redesign a Room With AI in 3 Steps
landing.how.step1.title: Upload a Photo of Your Room
landing.how.step1.desc: Snap a photo with your phone or use an existing shot — an empty room, a furnished room or a listing photo. We accept JPG, PNG, WEBP and HEIC up to 10MB. The AI reads your room’s dimensions, wall positions and light sources from that single image.
landing.how.step2.title: Pick a Room Type and a Design Style
landing.how.step2.desc: Tell the AI room designer what you are working on — living room, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, dining room, home office, kids room, basement, attic or study — then choose one of eight curated styles: Modern, Minimalist, Scandinavian, Japandi, Industrial, Bohemian, Coastal or Mid-century Modern. You can also type your own instruction, like “keep the sofa but make the walls warm oak”.
landing.how.step3.title: Generate and Download Your Design
landing.how.step3.desc: Hit Generate and get a photorealistic redesign in about 20 seconds. Download the result and use the before/after slider to see exactly what changed in your room.
landing.compare.title: AI Room Design vs. Hiring an Interior Designer
landing.compare.subtitle: Use the AI room design first, decide on a direction, then spend designer money only on the parts that need a human.
landing.faq.title: Questions? Answers.
landing.faq.description: Everything you need to know about redesigning your home with AI.
landing.faq.free.question: Is the AI room design tool free?
landing.faq.free.answer: Creating an account is free and includes one watermarked design. To download clean, full-size designs you use credits: one-time packs start at $5, and one standard room design costs about 14 credits.
landing.cta.headline: Turn One Room Photo Into a Real Design
landing.cta.subheadline: Upload one photo, choose a style, and generate a photorealistic redesign in about 20 seconds. Sign in and use credits when you are ready.
landing.pricing.title: Choose your plan.
landing.pricing.description: Buy credits once, or choose a monthly or yearly package for ongoing room designs.
landing.pricing.starter_desc: For trying out your first redesigns.
landing.blog.title: Design Ideas & Inspiration
landing.blog.description: Guides, room ideas and interior tips from the Redocor AI team.
landing.footer.tagline: Redesign any room in seconds — from a single photo.
landing.how.subtitle: No technical skills or architecture background required. Upload, choose, generate — that's the whole workflow.
landing.features.title: What This AI Room Designer Actually Does
landing.features.f1.title: Keeps Your Real Layout, Changes Everything Else
landing.features.f1.desc: Most AI image tools redraw a random room. This one starts from your photo: walls, windows, doors and the camera angle stay where they are, while furniture, finishes, colours and lighting are redesigned. That is the difference between a pretty picture and a design you can actually build.
landing.features.f2.title: Photorealistic Renders, Not Flat Sketches
landing.features.f2.desc: The engine renders light, shadow, fabric texture and material reflections — so you can judge a paint colour or a cabinet finish before spending money on either.
landing.features.f3.title: Runs in Your Browser, On Any Device
landing.features.f3.desc: Nothing to install, nothing to update. Open Redocor AI on your phone or laptop, upload a photo, and design on the spot — in a showroom, in a rental viewing, or standing in the room you are about to renovate.
landing.free.title: Simple Credit-Based Room Design
landing.free.subtitle: Your account's first design is free — after that, choose a package, and spend credits only when you generate:
landing.free.b1: One standard room design uses about 14 credits
landing.free.b3: Credits are available through one-time, monthly and yearly packages

landing.free.b6: Your first design is free and watermarked; paid designs download clean and full-size
landing.free.outro: Pick one-time credits for occasional projects, or save with a monthly or yearly package.

landing.faq.login.question: Do I need to create an account or log in?
landing.faq.login.answer: Only a free account — signing up also unlocks your free design. To generate more and download clean, full-size images, sign in and use credits from a one-time pack or a monthly/yearly package.
landing.faq.layout.question: Will the AI keep my room’s actual layout?
landing.faq.layout.answer: Yes. It preserves your walls, windows, doors and camera angle, and redesigns the furniture, finishes and lighting. You are looking at your own room, restyled — not a generic render.
landing.faq.room_types.question: What room types can it handle?
landing.faq.room_types.answer: Living rooms, bedrooms, kitchens, bathrooms, dining rooms, home offices, basements, attics, studies and kids rooms. Each room type has a dedicated guide in the section above.
landing.faq.styles.question: Which design styles are available?
landing.faq.styles.answer: Eight curated styles: Modern, Minimalist, Scandinavian, Japandi, Industrial, Bohemian, Coastal and Mid-century Modern. You can also describe a custom style in your own words and the AI will follow it.
landing.faq.phone.question: Can I use it on my phone?
landing.faq.phone.answer: Yes. It runs entirely in the browser — no app download. Upload straight from your camera roll.
landing.faq.time.question: How long does one design take?
landing.faq.time.answer: About 20 seconds per image. Each generation returns one room redesign and charges about 14 credits.
landing.faq.commercial.question: Can I use the renders commercially — for listings or client work?
landing.faq.commercial.answer: Commercial rights are included on paid plans. Real estate agents and interior designers use them for virtual staging and client pitches.
landing.changes.title: What the AI Changes — and What It Keeps
landing.changes.subtitle: A redesign you can trust starts with knowing exactly what will move. Nothing structural ever does.
landing.changes.change1: Furniture — swapped for style-matching pieces that fit the room
landing.changes.change2: Decor and textiles — rugs, cushions, curtains, artwork, plants
landing.changes.change3: Colors and finishes — wall paint, wood tones, cabinetry and metals
landing.changes.change4: Materials — the look of flooring, countertops and tile
landing.changes.change5: Lighting — fixtures and the overall light balance of the render
landing.changes.change6: Styling — how shelves, tables and surfaces are dressed
landing.changes.keep1: Walls and partitions — nothing structural moves
landing.changes.keep2: Windows and doors, exactly where they are
landing.changes.keep3: The room's real proportions and ceiling height
landing.changes.keep4: Your camera angle — the result is framed like your photo
landing.changes.keep5: Fixed installations — radiators, stairs and built-ins stay put
landing.changes.keep6: The room itself — a kitchen stays a kitchen
landing.styles.title: Eight Styles, One Photo
landing.styles.subtitle: Every style below is one tap away in the studio. Here is when to pick each one.
landing.styles.modern: Clean lines, a neutral base and purposeful contrast. The safe pick that makes almost any room look considered.
landing.styles.minimalist: Less, but better. Hidden storage, clear surfaces and breathing room — the style small rooms want.
landing.styles.scandinavian: Light woods, white walls and cozy textiles. Maximizes daylight — ideal for north-facing rooms.
landing.styles.japandi: Scandinavian calm meets Japanese restraint. Low furniture, natural textures and warm neutrals.
landing.styles.industrial: Exposed texture, dark metals, leather and concrete tones. Built for lofts and large open spaces.
landing.styles.bohemian: Layered rugs, plants, warm color and collected pieces. Personality-first, made for living rooms.
landing.styles.coastal: Whites, blues, rattan and breezy linen. Brings the feeling of daylight into city apartments.
landing.styles.midcentury: Tapered legs, warm walnut and organic curves. Timeless in bedrooms and dining rooms.

roompage.tips.title: Photo tips for {tips_for}
roompage.bathroom.title: AI Bathroom Design
roompage.bathroom.intro: Bathrooms are the smallest rooms with the most hard constraints — plumbing, tile and one small window. Upload one photo and see your bathroom restyled around the layout you already have: new tile looks, vanity styles, mirror and lighting ideas, all in about 20 seconds.
roompage.bathroom.meta_title: AI Bathroom Design — Redesign Your Bathroom From One Photo | Redocor AI
roompage.bathroom.meta_description: Upload one bathroom photo and get a photorealistic AI redesign in seconds — tile, vanity and lighting ideas that keep your real layout. First design free with a free account.
roompage.bathroom.tip1: Shoot facing the mirror and sink — it is the wall people look at most.
roompage.bathroom.tip2: Turn every light on so tile and grout colors read correctly.
roompage.bathroom.tip3: Close the shower curtain or door; the AI replaces it with a cleaner focal point.
roompage.bedroom.title: AI Bedroom Design
roompage.bedroom.intro: A bedroom redesign usually comes down to the bed wall, lighting and storage. From a single photo, the AI restyles your bedroom around the bed you already have — or swaps it — while keeping the room's real dimensions, window position and door swings. See a calm Scandinavian version and a warm mid-century version before you buy a single thing.
roompage.bedroom.meta_title: AI Bedroom Design — Restyle Your Bedroom From One Photo | Redocor AI
roompage.bedroom.meta_description: Turn one bedroom photo into a photorealistic redesign — new bed wall, lighting and storage ideas that fit your real room. First design free with a free account.
roompage.bedroom.tip1: Stand in the doorway and include the whole bed wall in frame.
roompage.bedroom.tip2: Daylight beats lamp light for judging wall and linen colors.
roompage.bedroom.tip3: Make the bed — the AI styles around the biggest object in the room.
roompage.living.title: AI Living Room Design
roompage.living.intro: The living room is where style is most visible and mistakes are most expensive. Upload one photo and compare eight styles on your actual sofa wall: same windows, same fireplace, same floor — different furniture, textiles and lighting. It is the fastest way to answer “would a dark green wall actually work?”
roompage.living.meta_title: AI Living Room Design — Restyle Your Living Room From One Photo | Redocor AI
roompage.living.meta_description: See your living room in eight different styles from one photo — same layout, new furniture and lighting. Photorealistic results in about 20 seconds.
roompage.living.tip1: Photograph the main seating wall straight on, at chest height.
roompage.living.tip2: Include the window — the AI keeps it and relights the room around it.
roompage.living.tip3: Do not move anything; clutter gets restyled too if it dominates the frame.
roompage.kitchen.title: AI Kitchen Design
roompage.kitchen.intro: Kitchen renovations are the most expensive room to get wrong. Before you talk to a contractor, test the look on your real kitchen: cabinet colors, countertop materials, backsplash tile and hardware — generated from one photo with your layout, appliances and window kept exactly where they are.
roompage.kitchen.meta_title: AI Kitchen Design — Try Cabinet and Countertop Looks From One Photo | Redocor AI
roompage.kitchen.meta_description: Upload one kitchen photo and see it restyled — cabinet colors, countertops and backsplash ideas that keep your real layout. First design free with a free account.
roompage.kitchen.tip1: Shoot from the main work aisle so counters and cabinets fill the frame.
roompage.kitchen.tip2: Clear the counters — you want to judge the kitchen, not last night's dishes.
roompage.kitchen.tip3: Keep small appliances in shot; the AI integrates them into the design.
roompage.dining.title: AI Dining Room Design
roompage.dining.intro: Dining rooms carry the occasions — holidays, dinners, homework. One photo is enough to see yours restyled around a different table shape, wall treatment and light fixture, with the chandelier position and window proportions you actually live with.
roompage.dining.meta_title: AI Dining Room Design — Restyle Your Dining Room From One Photo | Redocor AI
roompage.dining.meta_description: Turn a dining room photo into a photorealistic redesign — new table, wall and lighting ideas in your real space. First design free with a free account.
roompage.dining.tip1: Step back until the table and the wall behind it are both in frame.
roompage.dining.tip2: Include the light fixture — the AI keeps its position and restyles it.
roompage.dining.tip3: Set the table if you can; it gives the AI a sense of scale.
roompage.office.title: AI Home Office Design
roompage.office.intro: A home office has to work all day, not just look good in one. From one photo, test desk positions against the light, storage that fits your wall, and a style that makes the room a place you want to sit in — without moving a single outlet or radiator.
roompage.office.meta_title: AI Home Office Design — Design Your Home Office From One Photo | Redocor AI
roompage.office.meta_description: Upload a home office photo and get photorealistic redesigns — desk layout, storage and lighting ideas that fit your real room. First design free with a free account.
roompage.office.tip1: Shoot from the door with the desk and window both visible.
roompage.office.tip2: Note where the light falls — say “keep the desk facing the window” in instructions.
roompage.office.tip3: Include cable clutter; ask the AI to hide it with smarter storage.
roompage.basement.title: AI Basement Design
roompage.basement.intro: Basements are blank canvases with low ceilings and few windows. Show the AI what you have and get back a finished version — media room, gym, playroom or guest suite — that respects the real ceiling height, support walls and that one small window.
roompage.basement.meta_title: AI Basement Design — Visualize a Finished Basement From One Photo | Redocor AI
roompage.basement.meta_description: Turn a bare basement photo into a finished media room, gym or guest suite. Photorealistic AI design that keeps your real ceiling and walls. First design free with a free account.
roompage.basement.tip1: Use every light you have — basements are dim and color shifts.
roompage.basement.tip2: Include the ceiling; its height decides which furniture works.
roompage.basement.tip3: Say what you want it to become — “make this a cozy media room”.
roompage.attic.title: AI Attic Design
roompage.attic.intro: Attic rooms live and die by their slopes. The AI reads the angles from your photo and designs around them — beds under the eaves, built-ins on the short walls, skylights kept where they are — so you can see the room's best version before you insulate a single beam.
roompage.attic.meta_title: AI Attic Design — Design Around Sloped Ceilings From One Photo | Redocor AI
roompage.attic.meta_description: Upload an attic photo and see it finished — beds under the eaves, storage on the short walls, real skylights kept. First design free with a free account.
roompage.attic.tip1: Shoot the slope head-on so the AI reads the ceiling angles.
roompage.attic.tip2: Include the skylight if you have one — it stays and drives the light.
roompage.attic.tip3: Ask for low furniture: “everything under the slope line”.
roompage.study.title: AI Study Room Design

roompage.living.guide.title: Planning a living room redesign
roompage.living.guide.body:
Start from where people sit. A sofa needs 230–280 cm of wall or free floor, and the distance from the sofa to the TV should sit between 2 and 3 metres — close enough to read subtitles, far enough to see the whole picture. Keep walkways 75–90 cm wide so two people can pass without turning sideways, and let the rug anchor the seating: front legs of sofa and chairs on the rug, at least 150 cm wide for a sofa setup.

Layouts worth testing before you commit: the classic L-shape (sofa plus chaise or armchair), two sofas facing each other for conversation-heavy rooms, and a media-wall layout that hides cables and keeps the window wall free. A small living room usually gains more from one sofa plus two light armchairs than from a bulky sectional.

Spend in this order: paint and lighting first, then the sofa, then rugs and curtains, and styling last. The most common mistakes are pushing every piece flat against the walls, hanging the TV too high, and relying on a single ceiling light — layer a floor lamp and two table lamps instead.
roompage.bedroom.guide.title: Planning a bedroom redesign
roompage.bedroom.guide.body:
Place the bed first: the headboard goes on a solid wall, ideally opposite or diagonal from the door so the room feels calm when you walk in. Leave 60–70 cm of clearance on each side of the bed for making it and for nightstands, and never let a wardrobe door swing into the bed path — a 60 cm deep wardrobe needs another 60 cm of open floor in front.

Nightstand height should match the mattress top (within 5 cm), and a bench or chest at the foot of the bed adds storage without blocking the walkway. If the room is narrow, skip the footboard and let a low dresser do that job. Blackout curtains plus a 2700 K bedside lamp beat a bright ceiling light every time.

Budget tiers: bedding and curtains change the room the most per dollar, then a headboard upgrade, then lighting, and finally art. The recurring mistakes are rugs that stop under the bed frame (extend 45–60 cm beyond it), TVs opposite the pillow (light and noise), and storage bought before measuring the wall.
roompage.kitchen.guide.title: Planning a kitchen redesign
roompage.kitchen.guide.body:
The work triangle still rules: sink, stove and fridge should form a path of roughly 4–8 metres in total, with no leg crossing another. Keep 90–100 cm of clearance in front of every run and 100–120 cm where two people cook back-to-back; an island needs at least 90 cm on all sides to walk and open drawers.

Counter height sits at 90 cm standard, 82–85 cm if the main cook is under 165 cm. Plan a 40 cm landing zone on both sides of the stove and next to the fridge — trays and groceries need somewhere to land. Corner cabinets are where budgets die: either fit a carousel, or block the corner with a blind panel and use it for plumbing.

Material tiers: laminate counters and painted flat-panel doors on a budget; mid-tier butcher block or quartz-look porcelain; full quartz or stone only where you will keep it for a decade. The common mistakes are a backsplash that stops too low (take it to the upper cabinets), under-cabinet lighting skipped, and appliances ordered before the cabinet plan is final.
roompage.bathroom.guide.title: Planning a bathroom redesign
roompage.bathroom.guide.body:
In a small bathroom every centimetre is structural: a shower needs a minimum 80×80 cm tray (90×90 if you can), a vanity starts at 60 cm wide with the sink centre 40 cm from the wall, and the door must clear every fixture — a pocket door solves the swing problem in rooms under 4 m².

Group the wet zones on one wall: moving plumbing across the room can double the renovation cost, so keep toilet, shower and sink sharing a wet wall where possible. Tile is the main budget lever — large-format tiles on walls mean fewer grout lines and a calmer look, while the floor wants small or textured tiles for grip.

Spend on: a proper extractor fan (mould is a design failure, not a habit), one niche in the shower instead of racks, and a mirror-fronted cabinet for hidden storage. The recurring mistakes are mixing three metal finishes in one room, buying a vanity deeper than 50 cm for a narrow room, and light only from above the mirror — add sconces at face height.
roompage.dining.guide.title: Planning a dining room redesign
roompage.dining.guide.body:
Size the table to the room, not to the family: each diner needs 60 cm of table width, so a 120×80 cm table seats four, 150×90 seats six, and 180×90 seats eight. Chairs need 75 cm of clearance behind the table to slide out and walk, so measure the room minus 150 cm before falling in love with an eight-seater.

The pendant should hang 75–90 cm above the tabletop and span roughly half to two-thirds of the table width — one long pendant or two small ones for a rectangular top. If the table doubles as a work desk, add a dimmer so lunch light and task light can differ.

A rug under the table should extend 60 cm beyond it on all sides so chair legs never catch the edge. Budget tiers: a solid wood top with painted legs delivers 90% of the designer look at 40% of the price; spend the difference on the pendant and chairs, which you see every meal. Common mistakes: a pendant hung at standing head height, six chairs crammed around a four-seat table, and sideboards that block the serving path.
roompage.office.guide.title: Planning a home office redesign
roompage.office.guide.body:
Desk first: 120–140 cm wide by 60–80 cm deep fits a monitor at arm’s length with room for notes; anything deeper mostly stores clutter. Place the desk sideways to the window — facing it means glare, backing onto it means shadows on every call. Keep 100 cm behind the chair for getting up without turning.

Light in three layers: daylight from the side, a 4000 K ceiling fill, and a task lamp 30–40 cm from the keyboard. Acoustics matter more in video-call rooms than looks do — a rug, curtains and an upholstered chair cut echo enough to make a small room sound professional.

Storage ratio to aim for: two-thirds closed (drawers, cabinets) to one-third open shelving, or the room reads as cluttered within a month. Budget tiers: an electric standing desk is the only piece worth real money; everything else — lighting, acoustic panels, cable trays — is cheap and transformative. The recurring mistakes are a guest chair that blocks the only walkway, cables draped across the desk, and 6500 K white bulbs that make evening work feel like a hospital.
roompage.basement.guide.title: Planning a basement redesign
roompage.basement.guide.body:
Treat the ceiling as a design tool: painting walls and ceiling the same light tone makes a 220 cm basement feel a full head taller, while a two-tone split draws a line your eye follows downward. Zone the room around existing columns and the window wells — media corner in the darkest area, desk or guest zone near whatever daylight exists, and the utility area behind closed doors rather than drywalled over.

Materials must assume moisture: luxury vinyl plank over engineered wood, area rugs instead of wall-to-wall carpet, and metal or PVC storage near the floor drains. Recessed lights on dimmers spaced 180–240 cm apart replace the sun; add table lamps because basements read flat with ceiling light only.

Budget tiers: paint plus lighting plus one big rug transforms a basement for very little; furniture that survives a damp room (performance fabric, metal legs) is the mid-tier; built-ins are top-tier and only worth it once moisture is proven solved. Common mistakes: a dark palette turning the level into a cave, furniture arranged around the TV instead of the columns, and rugs laid before the floor has passed a full rainy season.
roompage.attic.guide.title: Planning an attic redesign
roompage.attic.guide.body:
Work with the slope, not against it: the usable zone is where headroom exceeds 150 cm, so put the bed or desk under the ridge and reserve the kneewalls — anything under 90 cm — for low storage, drawers or a window bench. A bed under the eaves wants its walking side on the tall wall, and built-ins should never exceed kneewall height or they fight the roofline.

Skylights are the attic’s currency: one over the task area is worth two anywhere else, and a skylight with a blackout blind makes the same room work for sleep. Keep the palette light and cool — the roof plane already warms the room visually, so white walls plus one wood tone read calm instead of cramped.

Budget tiers: freestanding low furniture first, custom kneewall drawers as the mid-tier, and dormers only if you are re-roofing anyway. The recurring mistakes are wardrobes placed against the short wall (doors will not open), pendant lights hanging where the sloped ceiling steals the headroom, and dark accent walls shrinking the only tall plane left.
roompage.study.guide.title: Planning a study room redesign
roompage.study.guide.body:
A study differs from a home office in one way: the books are the architecture. Plan shelving 25–30 cm deep for ordinary books (35 cm for art volumes), running along the wall you see on entering — a full wall of matched shelving reads intentional, while scattered cases read as clutter. Desk placement is a comfort decision: facing the door suits some people, facing a window suits others; sideways to the window suits everyone.

Quiet is built from soft surfaces: a rug under the desk chair, curtains instead of blinds, and upholstery anywhere you can add it. Task light comes from the side opposite your writing hand to kill shadows — a lamp 35–45 cm from the page, 3000–3500 K.

Budget tiers: budget-grade matched cases with trim painted to match the wall deliver the built-in look for a tenth of the price; spend the savings on the chair you sit in for hours. Common mistakes: shelves mounted directly above the desk (visual noise at eye level), a chair that rolls off the rug mid-thought, and glass-fronted doors on the messiest shelves.
roompage.kids.guide.title: Planning a kids room redesign
roompage.kids.guide.body:
Design for the child you will have in three years, not the one you have now: a bed that fits a 10-year-old, a desk that survives homework, and storage they can reach without a chair. Anchor every tall piece to the wall — dressers and shelves tip — and favour rounded corners and washable paint on the lower metre of the walls.

Zone the room into sleep, play and study even in 10 m²: the bed against the calmest wall, a rug that marks the play zone, and a desk near daylight. Keep the big elements neutral (walls, bed, storage) and let age-markers live in the swap layer — bedding, posters, lamp — so the room grows by replacing 20% of it, not all of it.

Budget tiers: a mid-tone neutral base with quality blackout curtains is the investment; open toy bins at child height are the cheap win; themed furniture (the race-car bed) is the trap — it dates in two years and costs triple. Common mistakes: storage too high for the child to use (so the floor becomes the shelf), one ceiling light doing everything, and cartoon murals on walls you will want to repaint long before they wear out.
roompage.planner.guide.title: How to plan a room layout that works
roompage.planner.guide.body:
Measure before you move anything: room dimensions, window and door swings, radiators, and power points — a plan that ignores a radiator is a plan that fails. Draw it at 1:50 on paper or in the planner, cut furniture templates to scale, and you can test an afternoon of layouts without lifting a sofa.

Three rules catch most bad layouts: keep walkways 75 cm wide, keep the entry sightline open (you should see into the room, not into the back of a wardrobe), and let each wall do one job — media, storage, conversation or view. Then test two or three arrangements and live with paper versions for a week before buying anything.

Budget-wise, planning is free and prevents the most expensive mistake in interior design: furniture that does not fit. Common planning failures: buying the sofa first and discovering the walkway later, ignoring door swings, and arranging everything around the TV when the room’s best asset is a window.
roompage.makeover.guide.title: What a one-weekend makeover can (and can’t) do
roompage.makeover.guide.body:
A makeover moves no walls: plumbing stays, kitchen runs stay, windows stay. What changes is everything your eye touches — wall colour, textiles, lighting, large furniture, styling. That is enough to make a room feel new, which is exactly why it is worth doing before any renovation.

Run it in sequence and the weekend is enough: day one, declutter and deep-clean (a half-empty room already looks twice as good); day two, paint the single wall that bothers you most; day two evening, rehang curtains higher and wider than the window. Only then buy — large pieces first, textiles second, styling last, on a 60/25/15 budget split.

The point of a photo-first makeover is deciding direction cheaply: generate three styles, live with them on screen for a day, and commit to one. Common mistakes: buying accent pieces before the big furniture is settled, repainting the whole room when one wall carries 80% of the problem, and skipping the declutter because it feels like it is not “design”.
